newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil soluble coffee exports fall in first half.
newsitem.headline: Brazil soluble coffee exports fall in first half.

text.p: Brazilian soluble coffee exports fell again in the first half of 1997 and other countries are slowly eating up Brazil's share of the pie in key markets such as Russia and the U.S., a soluble coffee official said.
Exports fell to 23,148 tonnes in the first half of the year, down 17.5 percent on the same period in 1996, said Roberto Paulo, vice-president of Brazil's Soluble Coffee Industry Association (Abics).
Export revenues meanwhile declined 26.1 percent to $153.13 million in the first six months of 1997.

The main reasons for Brazil's loss of competitiveness were the higher cost of raw materials for the soluble industry compared with other countries and heavy European Union taxes on imports of Brazilian soluble coffee, Paulo told reporters.
"This means that other competing countries are gaining in size," Paulo said.
Exports to Russia, the largest market for soluble coffee, fell 12.2 percent in January to June to 11,156 tonnes.
In the U.S., the second largest market for the industry, sales plummeted 44.7 percent to 3,751 tonnes in the first half and revenues were halved to $20.63 million.
"Consumption has not fallen, it's Brazil losing market share," Paulo said.
In Europe, where Brazilian soluble coffee imports are subject to a 10.1 percent tax, consumption has halved in the last five years, Paulo said.
"At the same time, there's been a frightening growth for exports from Columbia and Ecuador," he added.
Abics forecast that exports would total 57,500 tonnes in 1997, down slightly from 58,000 tonnes the previous year, and saw revenue of $383.70 million for the year, compared with $477 million in 1996.
Paulo said a Brazilian government proposal to lend the soluble industry some of its coffee stocks was still under review and needed to be approved by the Finance Ministry before being authorized.
"It's being studied, nothing has been defined yet," he said.
Under the plan, the soluble industry could borrow an estimated 700,000 bags of old government stocks and repay the coffee in kind with interest over a maximum of three years.
The total quantity being discussed, although still not confirmed, would represent a third of the sector's annual needs, Paulo said.
